claim: Phytophthora infestans triggered the Irish Great Famine in the 1840s.
source: Phytophthora infestans, the cause of potato late blight, is infamous for having triggered the Irish Great Famine in the 1840s.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract and is supported by historical knowledge and citations throughout the manuscript.

claim: Until the late 1970s, P. infestans diversity outside of its Mexican center of origin was low.
source: Until the late 1970s, P. infestans diversity outside of its Mexican center of origin was low, and one scenario held that a single strain, US-1, had dominated the global population for 150 years; this was later challenged based on DNA analysis of historical herbarium specimens.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous work (Goodwin et al., 1994) and is a summary of established knowledge in the field.

claim: The 19th century epidemic was caused by a unique genotype, HERB-1, that persisted for over 50 years.
source: We conclude that the 19th century epidemic was caused by a unique genotype, HERB-1, that persisted for over 50 years.
evidence: This conclusion is based on genomic data presented in the manuscript, including phylogenetic analyses and SNP data from herbarium samples.

claim: HERB-1 is distinct from all examined modern strains.
source: HERB-1 is distinct from all examined modern strains, but it is a close relative of US-1, which replaced it outside of Mexico in the 20th century.
evidence: This is supported by phylogenetic trees and genetic distance analyses presented in Figures 4 and 7.

claim: HERB-1 is a close relative of US-1.
source: HERB-1 is distinct from all examined modern strains, but it is a close relative of US-1, which replaced it outside of Mexico in the 20th century.
evidence: This is demonstrated by phylogenetic analyses showing HERB-1 and US-1 as sister groups in both mtDNA and nuclear genome trees.

claim: US-1 replaced HERB-1 outside of Mexico in the 20th century.
source: HERB-1 is distinct from all examined modern strains, but it is a close relative of US-1, which replaced it outside of Mexico in the 20th century.
evidence: This is inferred from the phylogenetic data and historical records showing US-1 dominance in the 20th century and HERB-1 presence in 19th century samples.

claim: HERB-1 and US-1 emerged from a metapopulation that was established in the early 1800s outside of the species' center of diversity.
source: We propose that HERB-1 and US-1 emerged from a metapopulation that was established in the early 1800s outside of the species' center of diversity.
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed by the authors based on divergence time estimates and phylogenetic relationships.

claim: P. infestans finally reached Europe in 1845.
source: In 1845, the oomycete P. infestans finally reached Europe, spreading rapidly from Belgium to other countries of mainland Europe and then to Great Britain and Ireland.
evidence: This is supported by historical records cited in the manuscript (Bourke, 1964; Reader, 2009).

claim: The Great Famine killed around 1 million people.
source: The subsequent Great Famine killed around 1 million people, and an additional million were forced to leave the island (Turner, 2005).
evidence: This is a historical fact supported by citation to Turner, 2005.

claim: An additional million people were forced to leave Ireland due to the Great Famine.
source: The subsequent Great Famine killed around 1 million people, and an additional million were forced to leave the island (Turner, 2005).
evidence: This is a historical fact supported by citation to Turner, 2005.

claim: The Irish population remains less than three quarters of what it was at the beginning of the 1840s.
source: Even today, the Irish population remains less than three quarters of what it was at the beginning of the 1840s.
evidence: This is a demographic fact that can be verified through historical population records.

claim: Late blight remains the most destructive disease of the third largest food crop.
source: Late blight remains the most destructive disease of the third largest food crop, resulting in annual losses of potatoes that would be sufficient to feed anywhere from 80 to many hundreds of millions of people (Fisher et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Fisher et al., 2012.

claim: P. infestans is thought to originate from Toluca Valley, Mexico.
source: The species is thought to originate from Toluca Valley, Mexico, where it infects wild relatives of potato, frequently undergoes sexual reproduction and co-occurs with the two closely related species P. mirabilis and P. ipomoeae (Tooley et al., 1985; Goodwin et al., 1994; Flier et al., 2003; Grünwald and Flier, 2005).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations (Tooley et al., 1985; Goodwin et al., 1994; Flier et al., 2003; Grünwald and Flier, 2005).

claim: The 240 Mb T30-4 reference genome of P. infestans is large compared to other species in the genus.
source: Compared to other species in the genus, the 240 Mb T30-4 reference genome of P. infestans is large, with three quarters of the genome consisting of repetitive DNA.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Haas et al., 2009.

claim: Three quarters of the P. infestans T30-4 genome consists of repetitive DNA.
source: Compared to other species in the genus, the 240 Mb T30-4 reference genome of P. infestans is large, with three quarters of the genome consisting of repetitive DNA.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Haas et al., 2009.

claim: RXLR proteins are encoded by about 550 genes in the P. infestans T30-4 genome.
source: RXLR proteins, the main class of host-translocated effectors, are encoded by about 550 genes in the P. infestans T30-4 genome.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Haas et al., 2009.

claim: Prior to the late 1970s, global P. infestans populations outside of South America and Mexico were dominated by a single clonal lineage with mitochondrial haplotype Ib called US-1.
source: Prior to the late 1970s, global P. infestans populations outside of South America and Mexico, the centers of diversity of the host and the pathogen, were dominated by a single clonal lineage that had the mitochondrial (mtDNA) haplotype Ib and was called US-1 (Goodwin et al., 1994).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Goodwin et al., 1994.

claim: Historic strains belonged to a mtDNA haplotype, Ia, that was distinct from that of the US-1 lineage.
source: The conclusion from these studies was that the historic strains belonged to a mtDNA haplotype, Ia, that was distinct from that of the US-1 lineage (Ristaino et al., 2001; May and Ristaino, 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Ristaino et al., 2001 and May and Ristaino, 2004.

claim: The previous conclusions about historic strains were based on only three mtDNA SNPs.
source: A caveat was that these far-reaching conclusions were based on only three mtDNA SNPs (Ristaino et al., 2001; May and Ristaino, 2004).
evidence: This is a critique of previous work supported by citations to Ristaino et al., 2001 and May and Ristaino, 2004.

claim: Eleven herbarium samples of infected potato and tomato leaves were shotgun-sequenced.
source: We have compared the genomes of 11 herbarium and 15 modern strains.
evidence: This is directly stated in the abstract and supported by Table 1 and methods.

claim: Fifteen modern strains were sequenced.
source: We have compared the genomes of 11 herbarium and 15 modern strains.
evidence: This is directly stated in the abstract and supported by Table 1 and methods.

claim: Herbarium samples were collected from continental Europe, Great Britain, Ireland, and North America in the period from 1845 to 1896.
source: We shotgun-sequenced 11 herbarium samples of infected potato and tomato leaves collected from continental Europe, Great Britain, Ireland, and North America in the period from 1845 to 1896, and extracted information on P. infestans mitochondrial and nuclear genomes.
evidence: This is supported by Table 1 which lists the provenance and collection years of samples.

claim: The median length of merged reads from herbarium samples was in the range of approximately 50–85 bp.
source: The median length of merged reads was in the range of approximately 50–85 bp (Figure 2A,B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2A and 2B.

claim: The fraction of P. infestans DNA in the herbarium samples was estimated to be between 1% and 20%.
source: Based on mapping against the reference genome, we estimated the fraction of P. infestans DNA in the samples to be between 1% and 20% (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2E.

claim: C-to-T was the predominant substitution at the 5′-end of molecules in herbarium samples.
source: Deamination of C to U in aDNA is highest at the first base (Briggs et al., 2007), and C-to-T was the predominant substitution at the 5′-end of molecules (Figure 2C,D).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2C and 2D and is consistent with known aDNA damage patterns.

claim: A total of 4.5 million non-redundant SNPs were called.
source: A total of 4.5 million non-redundant SNPs were called.
evidence: This is stated in the results section describing SNP calling.

claim: Eighty percent of all homozygous SNPs were found in at least eight samples.
source: Eighty percent of all homozygous SNPs were found in at least eight samples, and only 20% of all SNPs were found in fewer than 10 strains.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by Figure 3C.

claim: Historic samples did not fit into any of the previously recognized mtDNA haplotype groups (Ia, Ib, IIa and IIb), and instead formed an independent clade called HERB-1.
source: Surprisingly, a comparison of the complete mtDNA genomes revealed that the historic samples did not fit into any of these groups, and instead formed an independent clade, called HERB-1 from here on.
evidence: This is supported by the phylogenetic tree in Figure 4.

claim: Among the HERB-1 mtDNA genomes, there was a mean pair-wise difference of only 0.2 bp.
source: Among the HERB-1 mtDNA genomes, there were very few differences, with a mean pair-wise difference of only 0.2 bp, compared to 3.9 bp for the modern haplotype I strains, and 9.0 bp for modern haplotype II strains.
evidence: This is stated in the results section describing mtDNA phylogeny.

claim: Modern haplotype I strains had a mean pair-wise mtDNA difference of 3.9 bp.
source: Among the HERB-1 mtDNA genomes, there were very few differences, with a mean pair-wise difference of only 0.2 bp, compared to 3.9 bp for the modern haplotype I strains, and 9.0 bp for modern haplotype II strains.
evidence: This is stated in the results section describing mtDNA phylogeny.

claim: Modern haplotype II strains had a mean pair-wise mtDNA difference of 9.0 bp.
source: Among the HERB-1 mtDNA genomes, there were very few differences, with a mean pair-wise difference of only 0.2 bp, compared to 3.9 bp for the modern haplotype I strains, and 9.0 bp for modern haplotype II strains.
evidence: This is stated in the results section describing mtDNA phylogeny.

claim: DDR7602 (Germany) and LBUS5 (South Africa) are US-1 representatives.
source: The two US-1 representatives in our material, DDR7602 (Germany) and LBUS5 (South Africa), clustered together with the Ib reference genome and samples P6096 (Peru) and P1362 (Mexico) (Figure 4 and Figure 4—figure supplement 1), even though these last two samples had not been classified before as US-1 isolates.
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 4.

claim: US-1 is not a derivative of HERB-1.
source: Although the US-1 genotype is closely related to the herbarium strains, US-1 is not a derivative of HERB-1.
evidence: This is inferred from phylogenetic analyses showing HERB-1 and US-1 as sister groups with private substitutions in each lineage.

claim: HERB-1 and US-1 are sister groups that share a common ancestor.
source: Rather, HERB-1 and US-1 are sister groups that share a common ancestor.
evidence: This is supported by phylogenetic trees in Figures 4 and 7.

claim: There are three private substitutions that define the US-1 clade.
source: There are three private substitutions that define the US-1 clade, and two that define the HERB-1 clade.
evidence: This is stated in the results section describing mtDNA phylogeny.

claim: There are two private substitutions that define the HERB-1 clade.
source: There are three private substitutions that define the US-1 clade, and two that define the HERB-1 clade.
evidence: This is stated in the results section describing mtDNA phylogeny.

claim: All historic samples had a T at the position diagnostic for haplotype Ib.
source: In agreement with the previous report by Ristaino et al. (2001), all historic samples had a T at the position diagnostic for haplotype Ib (Figure 4—figure supplement 2), which distinguishes them from the US-1 lineage, which carries instead a C at this position.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: US-1 lineage carries a C at the position diagnostic for haplotype Ib.
source: In agreement with the previous report by Ristaino et al. (2001), all historic samples had a T at the position diagnostic for haplotype Ib (Figure 4—figure supplement 2), which distinguishes them from the US-1 lineage, which carries instead a C at this position.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: All HERB-1 strains showed significantly fewer mtDNA substitutions than modern strains with haplotype Ia or Ib (p=0.0003).
source: By calculating the nucleotide distance to the outgroup P17777, all HERB-1 strains were found to show significantly fewer mtDNA substitutions than modern strains with haplotype Ia or Ib (p=0.0003).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and shown in Figure 5.

claim: Sampling age of the strain and the number of mtDNA substitutions were highly correlated (r2 = 0.8).
source: Sampling age of the strain and the number of mtDNA substitutions were highly correlated (r2 = 0.8; Figure 5).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5.

claim: The mtDNA substitution rate was estimated to be 2.4 × 10−6 per site and year (1.5–3.3 × 10−6, 95% HPD).
source: From this procedure, we estimated the mtDNA substitution rate to be 2.4 × 10−6 per site and year (1.5–3.3 × 10−6, 95% HPD).
evidence: This is based on Bayesian framework analysis using BEAST.

claim: The mean divergence time for P. infestans and P. mirabilis was estimated to be 1318 years ago (853–1836 ya 95% HPD).
source: This rate resulted in a mean divergence time for P. infestans and P. mirabilis of 1318 years ago (ya) (853–1836 ya 95% HPD) and for P. infestans type I and type II mtDNA haplotypes of 460 ya (300–643 ya 95% HPD).
evidence: This is based on Bayesian framework analysis using BEAST and shown in Figure 6 and Table 3.

claim: The divergence time for P. infestans type I and type II mtDNA haplotypes was estimated to be 460 ya (300–643 ya 95% HPD).
source: This rate resulted in a mean divergence time for P. infestans and P. mirabilis of 1318 years ago (ya) (853–1836 ya 95% HPD) and for P. infestans type I and type II mtDNA haplotypes of 460 ya (300–643 ya 95% HPD).
evidence: This is based on Bayesian framework analysis using BEAST and shown in Figure 6 and Table 3.

claim: The origin of the 19th century herbarium clade was estimated to be around 182 ya (168–201 ya 95% HPD).
source: The origin of the 19th century herbarium clade was estimated to around 182 ya (168–201 ya 95% HPD) (Figure 6 and Table 3).
evidence: This is based on Bayesian framework analysis using BEAST and shown in Figure 6 and Table 3.

claim: The historic sample M-0182896 formed a distinct, isolated clade that appeared as a robust sister group to US-1 isolates DDR7602 and LBUS5 in phylogenetic trees.
source: In all cases, the HERB-1 representative, M-0182896, formed a distinct, isolated clade that appeared as a robust sister group to US-1 isolates DDR7602 and LBUS5.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7A, 7B, and Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: The two US-1 strains are both most closely related to HERB-1 and the most distinct among modern strains.
source: As a caveat, the random sampling of SNPs at heterozygous positions will inflate bootstrap support. Nevertheless, a heat map (Figure 7C) highlights that the two US-1 strains are both most closely related to HERB-1 and the most distinct among modern strains.
evidence: This is shown in the heat map in Figure 7C.

claim: No evidence was found for genes or sites that had experienced branch-specific positive selection in any of the lineages.
source: We did not find any evidence for genes or sites that had experienced branch-specific positive selection in any of the lineages, only a mosaic pattern with potentially positively selected genes shared across lineages.
evidence: This is based on PAML analysis described in the methods.

claim: The historic M-0182896 genome was apparently diploid.
source: Based on the shape and kurtosis of the distributions we concluded that the historic M-0182896 genome was apparently diploid.
evidence: This is based on analysis of read count distributions at biallelic SNPs shown in Figure 8.

claim: Of the modern genomes, only NL07434 and P17777 were diploid.
source: Of the modern genomes, only NL07434 and P17777 were diploid, whereas the majority, including the two US-1 strains DDR7602 and LBUS5 as well as P13527 and P13626 were triploid.
evidence: This is based on analysis of read count distributions at biallelic SNPs shown in Figure 8.

claim: The two US-1 strains DDR7602 and LBUS5 were triploid.
source: Of the modern genomes, only NL07434 and P17777 were diploid, whereas the majority, including the two US-1 strains DDR7602 and LBUS5 as well as P13527 and P13626 were triploid.
evidence: This is based on analysis of read count distributions at biallelic SNPs shown in Figure 8.

claim: One strain, 06_3928A, seemed to be tetraploid.
source: One strain, 06_3928A, even seemed to be tetraploid (Figure 8A,B and Figure 8—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on analysis of read count distributions at biallelic SNPs shown in Figure 8.

claim: M-0182896 had more than twice as many derived homozygous SNPs (8375) than DDR7602 (3440).
source: In agreement with the ploidy difference, M-0182896 had more than twice as many derived homozygous SNPs (8375) than DDR7602 (3440), regardless of annotation as synonymous, non-synonymous and non-sense (Figure 9A,B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 9 and supports the ploidy inference.

claim: All examined avirulence effector genes except Avr3b were present as full-length and intact coding sequences in the historic samples.
source: All examined avirulence effector genes except Avr3b were present as full-length and intact coding sequences in the historic samples (Table 4), without any frame shift or nonsense mutations.
evidence: This is shown in Table 4.

claim: The HERB-1 alleles of Avr1, Avr2, Avr3a and Avr4 were shared with those of the US-1 strain DDR7602.
source: The HERB-1 alleles of Avr1, Avr2, Avr3a and Avr4 were shared with those of the US-1 strain DDR7602 (Table 5—source data 1).
evidence: This is shown in Table 5 and Table 5—source data 1.

claim: The Avr1, Avr2, Avr3a and Avr4 alleles of HERB-1 are intact, presumably functional copies that are identical to ones that can be recognized by the matching R genes R1, R2, R3a and R4.
source: In conclusion, the Avr1, Avr2, Avr3a and Avr4 alleles of HERB-1 are intact, presumably functional copies that are identical to ones that can be recognized by the matching R genes R1, R2, R3a and R4 (Armstrong et al., 2005; van Poppel et al., 2008; Gilroy et al., 2011; Vleeshouwers et al., 2011).
evidence: This is based on sequence analysis and supported by citations to previous work on R gene recognition.

claim: Examination of Avr3a SNPs in the historic samples only revealed the AVR3aKI allele.
source: Examination of Avr3a SNPs in the historic samples only revealed the AVR3aKI allele, whereas both alleles were present in modern samples (Figure 10B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 10B.

claim: Both AVR3aKI and AVR3aEM alleles were present in modern samples.
source: Examination of Avr3a SNPs in the historic samples only revealed the AVR3aKI allele, whereas both alleles were present in modern samples (Figure 10B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 10B.

claim: Only R3 homologs that were distinct in sequence from R3a were found in de novo assembled reads from historic samples.
source: To confirm that the potato hosts of the historic strains lacked the ability to recognize AVR3aKI, we assembled de novo short reads from the historic samples and aligned them against the R3a sequence from modern potato (Huang et al., 2005). As expected, we only found R3 homologs that were distinct in sequence from R3a (Figure 10C).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 10C.

claim: The 19th century strains are closely related to the modern US-1 lineage, but are characterized by a single, distinct mtDNA haplotype, HERB-1.
source: Contrary to previous inferences (Ristaino et al., 2001; May and Ristaino, 2004), the 19th century strains are closely related to the modern US-1 lineage, but are characterized by a single, distinct mtDNA haplotype, HERB-1.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on phylogenetic analyses presented in the manuscript.

claim: Historic strains from different geographic locations all carried a mtDNA haplotype, HERB-1, that had not been recognized before.
source: Historic strains from different geographic locations all carried a mtDNA haplotype, HERB-1, that had not been recognized before (Figure 4).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4.

claim: The 19th century outbreak was a true pandemic of a rapidly spreading clonal genotype.
source: Although collected over a period of 50 years, the strains were distinguished from each other by few nuclear SNPs, indicating that the 19th century outbreak was a true pandemic of a rapidly spreading clonal genotype.
evidence: This is inferred from the low genetic diversity among HERB-1 samples.

claim: HERB-1 may have become extinct after the 19th century pandemic, possibly associated with the onset of resistance gene breeding in the 20th century.
source: That HERB-1 has so far not been found in any modern strain may point to its extinction after the 19th century pandemic, possibly associated with the onset of resistance gene breeding in the 20th century.
evidence: This is speculation based on the absence of HERB-1 in modern samples.

claim: The divergence of type I and type II mtDNA haplotypes coincides with the first contact between Americans and Europeans in Mexico.
source: Using the collection dates of the herbarium samples and isolation dates of the modern P. infestans strains, we estimated that type I and type II mtDNA haplotypes diverged close to the beginning of the 16th century (Figure 6 and Table 3). This coincides with the first contact between Americans and Europeans in Mexico, which potentially fuelled P. infestans population migration and expansion outside its center of diversity.
evidence: This is based on divergence time estimates and historical knowledge.

claim: A small P. infestans metapopulation was established at the periphery of its center of origin, or even outside Mexico, possibly in North America, some time before the first global P. infestans pandemic.
source: An alternative scenario is that a small P. infestans metapopulation was established at the periphery of its center of origin, or even outside Mexico, possibly in North America, some time before the first global P. infestans pandemic.
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed by the authors based on phylogenetic and divergence time data.

claim: The first lineage to spread from the metapopulation was HERB-1, which persisted globally for at least half a century.
source: The first lineage to spread from there was HERB-1, which persisted globally for at least half a century.
evidence: This is inferred from the presence of HERB-1 in samples from 1845 to 1896.

claim: Subsequently, the US-1 lineage expanded and spread, replacing HERB-1.
source: Subsequently, the US-1 lineage expanded and spread, replacing HERB-1 (Figure 11).
evidence: This is inferred from the phylogenetic data and historical records.

claim: R genes that confer resistance to historic P. infestans strains, such as R3a, were bred into cultivated potato Solanum tuberosum from the wild species S. demissum at the beginning of the 20th century.
source: Host R genes that confer resistance to historic P. infestans strains, such as R3a, were bred into cultivated potato Solanum tuberosum from the wild species S. demissum at the beginning of the 20th century, years after our youngest historic sample had been collected in 1896.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Hawkes, 1990.

claim: HERB-1 strains seem to have only the Avr3aKI allele, which interacts with the product of the R gene R3a to trigger a host immune response.
source: In agreement with the products of these R genes being able to recognize HERB-1 effectors, HERB-1 strains seem to have only the Avr3aKI allele, which interacts with the product of the R gene R3a to trigger a host immune response (Armstrong et al., 2005; Huang et al., 2005).
evidence: This is based on sequence analysis and supported by citations.

claim: The US-1 lineage also carries only the Avr3aKI allele.
source: While it is uncertain when HERB-1 was displaced by the US-1 lineage, the US-1 lineage also carries only the Avr3aKI allele (Armstrong et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Armstrong et al., 2005.

claim: The origin of the Avr3aEM allele that emerged to high frequency after the breeding of R3a into cultivated potatoes remains unclear.
source: The origin of the Avr3aEM allele that emerged to high frequency after the breeding of R3a into cultivated potatoes remains unclear.
evidence: This is stated as an open question in the discussion.

claim: Polyploidization could have provided an opportunity for US-1 isolates to enhance allelic diversity in the absence of frequent sexual reproduction.
source: Polyploidization could have provided an opportunity for US-1 isolates to enhance allelic diversity in the absence of frequent sexual reproduction, and could thus have contributed to their global success.
evidence: This is speculation based on the observed ploidy differences.

claim: Greater variation at effector genes in polyploid US-1 strains could have contributed to the replacement of HERB-1 soon after R genes from S. demissum and other wild species had been introduced into modern potato germplasm.
source: Therefore, if the major selection pressure that led to the replacement of HERB-1 by US-1 was the introduction of resistance gene breeding, greater variation at effector genes in polyploid US-1 strains could have contributed to the replacement of HERB-1 soon after R genes from S. demissum and other wild species had been introduced into modern potato germplasm.
evidence: This is speculation based on the observed ploidy differences and effector gene variation.

claim: The aDNA in the herbarium samples, which were about 150 years old, was remarkably well conserved.
source: The aDNA in the herbarium samples, which were about 150 years old, was remarkably well conserved, much better than most examples of aDNA from animals and humans, and only comparable with permafrost samples (Miller et al., 2008; Rasmussen et al., 2010).
evidence: This is based on the quality of DNA recovered and sequenced from herbarium samples.

claim: Knowledge of the genetics and geographic distribution of modern strains is insufficient to correctly infer the source of historic epidemics.
source: Our analyses not only highlight how knowledge of the genetics and geographic distribution of modern strains is insufficient to correctly infer the source of historic epidemics (Goodwin et al., 1994), but they also reveal the shortcomings of inferences that are based on a very small number of genetic markers in historic strains (Ristaino et al., 2001; May and Ristaino, 2004).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the comparison of current findings with previous work.

claim: Inferences based on a very small number of genetic markers in historic strains have shortcomings.
source: Our analyses not only highlight how knowledge of the genetics and geographic distribution of modern strains is insufficient to correctly infer the source of historic epidemics (Goodwin et al., 1994), but they also reveal the shortcomings of inferences that are based on a very small number of genetic markers in historic strains (Ristaino et al., 2001; May and Ristaino, 2004).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the comparison of current findings with previous work.

claim: The late blight outbreaks during the 19th century were a pandemic caused by a single P. infestans lineage.
source: With our much richer dataset, we could demonstrate that the late blight outbreaks during the 19th century were a pandemic caused by a single P. infestans lineage, but that this lineage was not the direct ancestor of the one that had come to dominate the global P. infestans population during much of the 20th century.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on genomic data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The 19th century lineage was not the direct ancestor of the one that had come to dominate the global P. infestans population during much of the 20th century.
source: With our much richer dataset, we could demonstrate that the late blight outbreaks during the 19th century were a pandemic caused by a single P. infestans lineage, but that this lineage was not the direct ancestor of the one that had come to dominate the global P. infestans population during much of the 20th century.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on genomic data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Infected plant specimens stored in herbaria around the world are a largely untapped source to learn about events that affected millions of people during our recent history.
source: Infected plant specimens stored in herbaria around the world are thus a largely untapped source to learn about events that affected millions of people during our recent history.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the successful analysis of herbarium samples in this study.

claim: Initial introgression of the R3 locus from S. demissum was based on the resistance phenotype conferred by the R3a gene.
source: Based on the absence of an Avr3b gene in HERB-1, we conclude that initial introgression of the R3 locus from S. demissum was based on the resistance phenotype conferred by the R3a gene.
evidence: This is inferred from the absence of Avr3b in HERB-1 and the presence of Avr3a.

claim: The presence of R3b must have been irrelevant until P. infestans strains carrying Avr3b emerged.
source: The R3 phenotype scored during the initial introgression must have been the recognition of Avr3a by R3a, and the presence of R3b must have been irrelevant until P. infestans strains carrying Avr3b emerged.
evidence: This is inferred from the absence of Avr3b in HERB-1.

claim: P. infestans spread rapidly from Belgium to other countries of mainland Europe and then to Great Britain and Ireland in 1845.
source: In 1845, the oomycete P. infestans finally reached Europe, spreading rapidly from Belgium to other countries of mainland Europe and then to Great Britain and Ireland.
evidence: This is supported by historical records cited in the manuscript.

claim: The impact of the epidemic reached catastrophic levels in Ireland, where the population was more dependent on potato for their subsistence than in other parts of Europe.
source: The impact of the epidemic reached catastrophic levels in Ireland, where the population was more dependent on potato for their subsistence than in other parts of Europe (Bourke, 1964; Reader, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Bourke, 1964 and Reader, 2009.

claim: P. infestans infects wild relatives of potato in Toluca Valley, Mexico.
source: The species is thought to originate from Toluca Valley, Mexico, where it infects wild relatives of potato, frequently undergoes sexual reproduction and co-occurs with the two closely related species P. mirabilis and P. ipomoeae (Tooley et al., 1985; Goodwin et al., 1994; Flier et al., 2003; Grünwald and Flier, 2005).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: P. infestans frequently undergoes sexual reproduction in Toluca Valley, Mexico.
source: The species is thought to originate from Toluca Valley, Mexico, where it infects wild relatives of potato, frequently undergoes sexual reproduction and co-occurs with the two closely related species P. mirabilis and P. ipomoeae (Tooley et al., 1985; Goodwin et al., 1994; Flier et al., 2003; Grünwald and Flier, 2005).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: P. infestans co-occurs with the two closely related species P. mirabilis and P. ipomoeae in Toluca Valley, Mexico.
source: The species is thought to originate from Toluca Valley, Mexico, where it infects wild relatives of potato, frequently undergoes sexual reproduction and co-occurs with the two closely related species P. mirabilis and P. ipomoeae (Tooley et al., 1985; Goodwin et al., 1994; Flier et al., 2003; Grünwald and Flier, 2005).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: In its center of origin, P. infestans is characterized by high levels of genetic and phenotypic diversity.
source: In its center of origin, P. infestans is characterized by high levels of genetic and phenotypic diversity (Grünwald and Flier, 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Grünwald and Flier, 2005.

claim: RXLR effectors that can be recognized by plant immune receptors, known as Resistance (R) proteins, are said to have 'avirulence' activity.
source: RXLR effectors that can be recognized by plant immune receptors, known as Resistance (R) proteins, are said to have 'avirulence' activity.
evidence: This is established knowledge in plant pathology.

claim: Upon introduction of a cognate R gene into the host population, avirulence effectors become a liability for the pathogen, and natural selection favors the spread of pseudogenized or mutated alleles.
source: Upon introduction of a cognate R gene into the host population, such avirulence effectors become a liability for the pathogen, and natural selection favors the spread of pseudogenized or mutated alleles (Vleeshouwers et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Vleeshouwers et al., 2011 and is established knowledge in plant pathology.

claim: The detailed descriptions and drawings of Heinrich Anton de Bary and the reports of several other pioneers of plant pathology leave no doubt that the 19th century blight epidemic was triggered by P. infestans.
source: The detailed descriptions and drawings of Heinrich Anton de Bary and the reports of several other pioneers of plant pathology leave no doubt that the 19th century blight epidemic was triggered by P. infestans (de Bary, 1876; Bourke, 1964).
evidence: This is supported by citations to historical work.

claim: May and Ristaino (2004) speculated that the 19th century and US-1 lineages represented two independent epidemics of divergent lineages that had both originated in South America and spread from there to North America and Europe.
source: Because Ia was at the time not only the predominant haplotype in the Toluca Valley in Mexico (Gavino and Fry, 2002; Flier et al., 2003), but had also been found in South America (Perez et al., 2001), May and Ristaino (2004) speculated that the 19th century and US-1 lineages represented two independent epidemics of divergent lineages that had both originated in South America and spread from there to North America and Europe.
evidence: This is a summary of previous speculation supported by citations.

claim: Samples P6096 (Peru) and P1362 (Mexico) had not been classified before as US-1 isolates.
source: The two US-1 representatives in our material, DDR7602 (Germany) and LBUS5 (South Africa), clustered together with the Ib reference genome and samples P6096 (Peru) and P1362 (Mexico) (Figure 4 and Figure 4—figure supplement 1), even though these last two samples had not been classified before as US-1 isolates.
evidence: This is stated in the results section.

claim: The molecular clock hypothesis for the modern strains could not be rejected at a 5% significance level (p=0.12).
source: The molecular clock hypothesis for the modern strains could not be rejected at a 5% significance level (p=0.12).
evidence: This is based on statistical testing described in the methods.

claim: R3b is within 0.4 cM of R3a in the complex R3 locus.
source: However, R3b, the matching R gene of Avr3b, is within 0.4 cM of R3a in the complex R3 locus (Li et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Li et al., 2011.

claim: Only the AVR3aKI type triggers signaling by the resistance protein R3a.
source: The two major Avr3a alleles encode secreted proteins that differ in two amino acids in their effector domains: AVR3aKI and AVR3aEM (Figure 10A, and Figure 10—figure supplement 1). Only the AVR3aKI type triggers signaling by the resistance protein R3a (Armstrong et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Armstrong et al., 2005.

claim: The R3a gene was introduced into modern potato from S. demissum at the beginning of the 20th century.
source: The R3a gene was introduced into modern potato from S. demissum at the beginning of the 20th century, providing modern potato with resistance against the P. infestans strains prevalent at the time (Hawkes, 1990; Gebhardt and Valkonen, 2001; Huang et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Hawkes, 1990; Gebhardt and Valkonen, 2001; Huang et al., 2005.

claim: Strains homozygous for Avr3aEM, which avoids R3a-mediated detection of the pathogen, appeared later.
source: Strains homozygous for Avr3aEM, which avoids R3a-mediated detection of the pathogen, appeared later; US-1 isolates lack Avr3aEM (Armstrong et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Armstrong et al., 2005.

claim: US-1 isolates lack Avr3aEM.
source: Strains homozygous for Avr3aEM, which avoids R3a-mediated detection of the pathogen, appeared later; US-1 isolates lack Avr3aEM (Armstrong et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Armstrong et al., 2005.

claim: Nineteenth-century samples of potato and tomato leaves with P. infestans lesions were obtained from the herbaria of the Botanische Staatssammlung München and the Kew Royal Botanical Gardens.
source: Nineteenth-century samples of potato and tomato leaves with P. infestans lesions were obtained from the herbaria of the Botanische Staatssammlung München and the Kew Royal Botanical Gardens (Table 1 and Figure 1).
evidence: This is stated in the methods section and shown in Table 1.

claim: DNA was extracted under clean room conditions.
source: DNA was extracted under clean room conditions and two genomic libraries were prepared from each sample for Illumina sequencing.
evidence: This is stated in the methods section.

claim: Two genomic libraries were prepared from each sample for Illumina sequencing.
source: DNA was extracted under clean room conditions and two genomic libraries were prepared from each sample for Illumina sequencing.
evidence: This is stated in the methods section.

claim: The preparations were expected to comprise P. infestans DNA, host DNA from potato or tomato as well as DNA from microbes that had colonized either the living material at the time of its collection, or the dried material during its storage in the herbaria.
source: The preparations were expected to comprise P. infestans DNA, host DNA from potato or tomato as well as DNA from microbes that had colonized either the living material at the time of its collection, or the dried material during its storage in the herbaria.
evidence: This is stated in the methods section.

claim: The combination of uracil-DNA-glycosylase (UDG) and endonuclease VIII reduces the overall per-base error rate to as low as one 20th of unrepaired aDNA.
source: The combination of uracil-DNA-glycosylase (UDG) and endonuclease VIII, which removes uracil residues and repairs abasic sites, reduces the overall per-base error rate to as low as one 20th of unrepaired aDNA (Briggs et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Briggs et al., 2010.

claim: Ancient DNA fragments are typically shorter than 100 bp.
source: Ancient DNA fragments are typically shorter than 100 bp (Pääbo, 1989), and paired-end reads of 100 bases each will therefore substantially overlap.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Pääbo, 1989 and is established knowledge in aDNA research.

claim: Merging of short-insert libraries considerably decreases the error-rate and also generates sequences that reflect the original molecule length.
source: Merging of short-insert libraries considerably decreases the error-rate and also generates sequences that reflect the original molecule length (Kircher, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Kircher, 2012.
